bull_thesis:
The event works if the coffee spin-off actually happens on something close to the stated timetable and the market then values the two halves the way it values their peers. Keurig Dr Pepper has already done the hard, irreversible part: the $18 billion cash purchase of JDE Peet's, the Dutch coffee group behind Jacobs, Douwe Egberts and Peet's, settled on 1 April 2026 with 96.22% of shares tendered, rose to 97.75% in the follow-on window, delisted from Euronext Amsterdam on 30 April 2026, and the company implemented a post-closing demerger whose stated purpose is to enable the separation. That is completed legal machinery, not an intention.

What is left is a tax-free spin-off of the coffee business, leaving a North American refreshment-beverage company behind. The bull case is a sum-of-the-parts case (valuing each business separately and adding them up). Beverage Co. would be a pure-play North American drinks company built on Dr Pepper, the number-two carbonated soft drink in the United States and still gaining share, plus Canada Dry, Snapple and a growing energy portfolio, distributed through a direct-store-delivery network that is expensive for anyone to replicate. On roughly $13.3 billion of 2027 revenue at a high-twenties margin, that is about $3.85 billion of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation. Peers of that quality trade at 15 to 19 times that measure; today the whole company trades at roughly 9.8 times consensus 2027 earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, and about 12.3 times 2027 earnings per share of $2.53, against packaged-food and drinks peers at 17 to 20 times earnings.

Global Coffee Co. would be one of the largest coffee businesses in the world by volume, combining the Keurig single-serve system in North America with JDE Peet's international roast-and-ground and instant portfolio, at roughly $16.4 billion of revenue. It is a slower, more commodity-exposed business, but the market pays 9 to 11 times cash profit for that kind of asset, and JDE Peet's itself was taken out around the upper end of that band.

The conditions the bull case depends on are specific and checkable. First, the company has to name a chief executive for the coffee business and file the registration statement that turns 'early 2027' into an actual distribution date. Second, leverage has to come down: management has said plainly that separation timing depends on 'achievement of key milestones, including appropriate leverage levels at each company,' and combined borrowings sit near 4.5 times cash profit. Third, green-coffee costs, which have been compressing US coffee results all year, need to stabilise so the coffee company can be floated on a clean multiple rather than a trough one. If all three land, the parts are worth roughly $42 a share on favourable assumptions, and the operating business is meanwhile holding up: first-quarter 2026 net sales rose 9.4% to $3.98 billion with adjusted earnings of $0.39 a share, guidance for $25.9 to $26.4 billion of 2026 net sales and low-double-digit constant-currency earnings growth has been reaffirmed twice, and the company has met or beaten estimates in each of the last four quarters.
bear_thesis:
The event fails, in the way these usually fail, by simply not arriving on time. There is no date. The separation was described as operationally ready 'by end of 2026' in October 2025, still carried a year-end 2026 target in February 2026, and became 'targeted for early 2027' on 23 June 2026 — one slip already, with the target explicitly conditioned on leverage levels and market conditions the company does not control. Nothing binds the company to a distribution date, no registration statement for the coffee company has been filed, and there is no contractual payout of any kind. This is a goal, not a schedule.

The leadership prerequisite has just been vacated for the second time in nine months. Sudhanshu Priyadarshi, originally slated to run the coffee company, was moved out of the chief financial officer role in November 2025 and off that plan. Rafael Oliveira was named chief executive of the future coffee company on the day the acquisition closed in April 2026, and told the company in June 2026 he was leaving at the end of July for an outside role. The search has restarted. Bank of America called it a setback precisely because the timetable now depends on hiring. A company cannot run a spin-off roadshow for a business with no chief executive, so the practical earliest date is later than the stated one.

The deeper problem is what the common shareholder actually owns. The acquisition was not funded with debt and ordinary shares. Three claims now sit ahead of or alongside the common: about $9 billion of new long-term debt plus roughly $5 billion of assumed JDE Peet's bonds; $4.5 billion of Series A convertible perpetual preferred stock co-led by Apollo and KKR, upsized from $3 billion on 23 February 2026, paying 4.75% a year, ranking senior for dividends and on liquidation with a $1,000-per-share liquidation preference, never maturing, and carrying registration rights that give the holders a path to sell; and a pod-manufacturing joint venture into which Apollo, KKR and Goldman Sachs Asset Management put about $4 billion for 49%, showing up as $3.9 billion of minority interest at 31 March 2026. Note what was sold there: half the economics of K-Cup pod manufacturing, the highest-margin part of the coffee business. Roughly $36 billion of debt, preferred and minority claims now stands between enterprise value and the share. A parts valuation that subtracts only bonds overstates the answer by about $6 a share.

That leverage — near 4.5 times cash profit — is what turns a dull staples stock into a levered call option. A 10% shortfall in profit combined with one turn of multiple compression takes roughly a third off the equity. And the profit shortfall has a live source: elevated green-coffee costs have been pressuring the US coffee business all year, and the company has just multiplied its coffee exposure. Free cash flow yield is about 3.7% and interest costs have risen sharply.

Finally, the index-flow leg of the thesis points the wrong way. When a spin-off happens, funds that track the parent's index are typically forced to sell the newly distributed company. That creates a discount in the coffee spin-off after the fact — it is not a tailwind for shares held beforehand. If anything, holders face a dividend that must be split between two companies (the current $0.23 quarterly payout, $0.92 a year, yields about 3.0%) and an income-oriented shareholder base with no natural reason to stay. What confirms the bear case: the separation target moving past mid-2027, a coffee chief executive still unnamed by the year-end 2026 results, or a 2026 guidance cut on coffee input costs at the 6 August 2026 second-quarter report.
sop_bull: Favourable parts valuation, roughly $42 a share. Beverage Co.: about $13.3 billion of 2027 revenue at a 30% margin gives roughly $4.0 billion of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation; at 16 times, the multiple a high-quality North American drinks pure-play with mid-single-digit growth can command, that is about $64 billion of enterprise value. Global Coffee Co.: about $16.4 billion of revenue at a 22% margin gives roughly $3.6 billion of the same measure; at 11 times, in line with where JDE Peet's itself was acquired, that is about $39.6 billion. Deduct roughly $2 billion for separation costs and stranded overhead, giving about $101.6 billion of combined enterprise value. Subtract net debt of about $26 billion (assuming two more years of cash generation reduces it), the $4.5 billion convertible perpetual preferred, and the $3.9 billion pod joint-venture minority interest, and about $67 billion of common equity remains across roughly 1.36 billion shares — near $49. Haircut that back to about $42 to allow for the convertible preferred converting into shares and for the debt allocation between the two companies landing less favourably than assumed.
sop_bear: Adverse parts valuation, roughly $26 a share — and this, not the $28.50 the board file carried, is the honest downside floor. Beverage Co.: about $12.8 billion of revenue at a 29% margin gives roughly $3.7 billion of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation; at 13 times, reflecting a company still carrying separation overhang, that is about $48.1 billion. Global Coffee Co.: coffee profit misses on elevated green-coffee costs at roughly $3.1 billion; at 8.5 times, the multiple a leveraged, slower-growth coffee company earns without a chief executive or a track record, that is about $26.4 billion. Deduct $2.5 billion of separation and stranded costs for about $72 billion of enterprise value. Subtract net debt of about $28.5 billion (leverage stays near 4.5 times because the spin slips), the $4.5 billion preferred and the $3.9 billion pod minority, leaving about $35 billion of common equity, or roughly $26 a share. Three independent checks land in the same place: the 52-week low is $24.88, $26 is about 10.3 times 2027 consensus earnings of $2.53, and the $0.92 annual dividend yields 3.5% there — the level at which income buyers historically step in. Crucially, this is a valuation floor, not a hard one: there is no deal-break price, no cash backstop and no contractual payout beneath this stock.
sop_breakdown: Base case of about $36 a share, the probability-weighted midpoint of the two cases (roughly 55% weight on the favourable path, 45% on the adverse one). Beverage Co. contributes about $3.85 billion of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation at 15 times, or roughly $57.8 billion of enterprise value — a little over $20 a share after its share of the claims. Global Coffee Co. contributes about $3.35 billion at 10 times, or roughly $33.5 billion. Less about $2.5 billion of separation and stranded costs, combined enterprise value is close to $88.8 billion. From that, subtract roughly $27.5 billion of net debt, the $4.5 billion convertible perpetual preferred and the $3.9 billion pod joint-venture minority interest — about $35.9 billion of claims ahead of the common — leaving roughly $52.9 billion of equity across 1.36 billion shares. That is about $38 on those multiples; rounding down to $36 reflects the real possibility that the timetable slips again and that the debt split between the two companies is less shareholder-friendly than assumed. For reference, the street's median target is $37 and the consensus is $34.40, so this base case sits inside, not outside, what is already published.
risk_reward: About 1.3 to 1, not the 2.8 to 1 carried in the board file. From $31.12, the upside to the $36 base case is roughly 16%, and to the $37 street median target roughly 19%. The downside to the honest floor of $26 is roughly 16%. The board file's 2.8-to-1 came from pairing a top-of-range $37.70 target with a $28.50 floor, and that floor is simply the 200-day moving average ($28.62) rather than anything that backstops value. Correct the floor for the $4.5 billion of perpetual preferred and $3.9 billion of pod joint-venture minority interest that sit ahead of the common, and the asymmetry is roughly symmetric. This is a fairly priced situation with an unscheduled catalyst, not a defined-risk special situation.
catalyst_summary: The tax-free spin-off of the coffee business is real and structurally in motion but carries no date: 'targeted for early 2027' as of 23 June 2026, already pushed back from an end-of-2026 goal, conditioned on leverage and market conditions, with the coffee chief executive seat vacant since the end of July 2026 and no registration statement filed. Upside to about $36 against a soft floor near $26 — roughly 1.3 to 1.
dated_milestone: The only firm date on the calendar is second-quarter 2026 results, released before the market opens on Thursday 6 August 2026, with a call at 8:00 a.m. Eastern hosted by chief executive Tim Cofer and chief financial officer Anthony DiSilvestro. That is the first full quarter including JDE Peet's and the next point at which the separation timetable, the debt split and the dividend policy can be updated. The separation itself has no date: management's language on 23 June 2026 was 'targeted for early 2027,' subject to milestones including appropriate leverage at each company and supportive market conditions. Completed and verified dates behind us: tender offer settlement 1 April 2026 at 96.22% tendered; post-closing acceptance to 97.75% settled 15 April 2026; Euronext Amsterdam delisting 30 April 2026; bridge loan repaid 30 March 2026.
forcing_function:
Two prerequisites, neither of which yet exists, are what would convert this from a story into a dated event. First, the naming of a chief executive for Global Coffee Co. The board reopened that search on 23 June 2026 under chairman Pamela Patsley after Rafael Oliveira — named to the role only in April 2026 — resigned effective the end of July. No spin-off gets a distribution date before its chief executive is hired. Second, the filing of the registration statement for the coffee company with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the document that sets the record and distribution dates and publishes standalone financials, the debt allocation and the dividend policy for both halves. That filing is the moment the market can finally price the two businesses separately, and it is the true forcing event.

A third, weaker trigger is deleveraging itself: management has tied timing to 'appropriate leverage levels at each company,' so each quarter of debt paydown mechanically brings the date closer. The nearest checkpoint on all three is the 6 August 2026 second-quarter report.
consensus_delta:
Here is the uncomfortable part: on the parts valuation, we largely agree with Wall Street, which is exactly what an expectations-arbitrage framework is supposed to flag as a warning. Consensus sits at a $34.40 average and a $37 median target, with a $39 high and a $28 low. JPMorgan raised its target to $38 on 23 July 2026, Bank of America added the stock to its high-conviction list on 21 July 2026, and Barclays' own parts work points above the current price on improving leverage and what it calls waning transaction uncertainty. The board file's $37.70 target is effectively the street median. There is no variant view in buying a sum-of-the-parts story that every major broker has already published.

Where we do disagree with the street is on two mechanics it appears to be waving through. First, the capital structure. Most published parts work deducts bond debt and stops there. It does not fully deduct the $4.5 billion Series A convertible perpetual preferred — senior, never-maturing, 4.75%, participating in common dividends on an as-converted basis, with a $1,000-per-share liquidation preference — or the $3.9 billion minority interest created when Apollo, KKR and Goldman Sachs Asset Management bought 49% of the pod-manufacturing joint venture for about $4 billion. Those are permanent claims on the very cash flows the parts valuation is capitalising, worth roughly $6 a share. The street's enthusiasm was priced against an enterprise value that is understated.

Second, timing. The street is underwriting 'early 2027' as though it were scheduled. It is not. The target has already moved once, it is conditioned on leverage the company is still working down, and the three price-target raises all came after the designated coffee chief executive resigned — meaning the market raised numbers on the parts while ignoring the process. Our view is that mid-to-late 2027 is at least as likely as early 2027, and every quarter of delay is a quarter of carrying leverage near 4.5 times through a period of elevated coffee costs. The discount is real; the reason it exists is also real, and the street is treating it as friction rather than as risk.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months carry more downside surprise than upside. The immediate one is second-quarter results on 6 August 2026, three days from this review. It is the first full quarter with JDE Peet's consolidated, and green-coffee costs have been elevated all year — the stock has already underperformed the consumer-staples sector over the past quarter on exactly that concern, falling from roughly $33.30 in early July to $31.12, with a 52-week range of $24.88 to $35.94. Consensus expects $0.55 of diluted earnings per share against $0.49 a year ago. A guidance trim on coffee input costs would hit a stock that has just absorbed three bullish broker notes, which is the setup that produces the sharpest single-day falls.

The structural pressure is the balance sheet. Total debt stood at $25.7 billion against $0.9 billion of cash at 31 March 2026, before the April closing consumed the roughly $18 billion of acquisition funding held in current assets, and combined leverage is targeted near 4.5 times cash profit including about $5 billion of assumed JDE Peet's bonds. On top of that sits $214 million a year of preferred dividends at 4.75% on $4.5 billion, plus the 49% of pod-manufacturing profit that now belongs to outside investors. Free cash flow yield is about 3.7% and the ordinary dividend costs roughly $1.25 billion a year. That is a thin cushion for deleveraging on the timetable the spin requires.

The third risk is integration itself, conducted with a hole at the top of the coffee business. Rafael Oliveira left at the end of July 2026; Tim Cofer is running coffee in the interim while preparing to lead the other company. Cross-border integrations of this size lose people, and this one is losing them at the moment the acquired business is meant to be readied for its own listing. Any of these — a coffee-cost guidance cut, a leverage-driven delay, or an integration stumble — pushes the separation date out without breaking the thesis, which is the worst outcome for a position sized to an event: the story survives, the clock does not.
positioning_washout:
The shareholder base is the wrong one for what this company is becoming, and the separation is what forces the change. Keurig Dr Pepper has been owned as a defensive staples holding paying a $0.23 quarterly dividend, $0.92 a year, for a yield near 3.0%, with modest leverage. It is now a 4.5-times-levered company mid-way through splitting in two, with $8.5 billion of senior and minority capital from private-credit sponsors in its structure.

Three mechanical selling pressures are queued. First, the dividend must be divided between two companies at separation and neither policy has been announced. Income mandates that require a stated yield cannot hold a position through an unannounced payout reset, and a slower-growth coffee company carrying its share of the debt is unlikely to fund the income half of that split generously.

Second — and this is the point the board file has backwards — index flow works against the parent, not for it. Funds tracking the S&P 500 hold Keurig Dr Pepper because it is in the index. When the coffee company is distributed, those funds receive shares in a company that is not in their benchmark, and unless the index committee adds it they must sell mechanically, often within days. That forced supply creates a discount in the newly listed coffee company; it does no favours for the shares held beforehand. The genuine forced-seller opportunity in this situation is a trade in the spin-off, six or more months from now, and it is not available today.

Third, the convertible perpetual preferred carries registration rights, giving Apollo, KKR and the co-investors a defined path to convert and sell. That is a supply overhang with no fixed date, sitting above a share count of roughly 1.36 billion. The washout that would make this interesting — income holders capitulating into a dividend reset, taking the stock toward the $26 to $28 area — has not happened. Buying before it does is paying for a re-rating while the sellers are still in the building.
moderator_conclusion:
The verdict is to wait, not to pass. This is a genuine transformation, executed so far with real competence, priced at a genuine discount — and it has no date.

Start with what is verified. The enabling acquisition is finished: $18 billion for JDE Peet's, settled 1 April 2026 with 96.22% of shares tendered, taken to 97.75%, delisted from Amsterdam on 30 April 2026, with a post-closing demerger implemented specifically to make the separation possible. That is not a promise, it is completed corporate machinery, and it distinguishes this from the average 'strategic review' story. Operations are holding too — first-quarter 2026 net sales up 9.4% to $3.98 billion, guidance reaffirmed twice including on the day the coffee chief executive's resignation was disclosed, four straight quarters at or above estimates.

Now the part that decides the sizing. The event we are actually being asked to underwrite — the coffee spin-off — is not scheduled. It was 'operationally ready by end of 2026' in October 2025 and became 'targeted for early 2027' on 23 June 2026, explicitly subject to leverage levels and market conditions. No registration statement has been filed. The chief executive designated to run the coffee company resigned at the end of July 2026, the second time that seat has emptied in nine months, and the search has restarted. Companies do not set distribution dates for businesses without chief executives. That is a soft, non-binding catalyst with no contractual payout, and in a book built on dated events it does not earn a front-foot allocation.

The floor is the second problem. The board file carried $28.50; that is the 200-day moving average, a chart level. Beneath this stock there is no deal-break price, no cash backstop and no contractual payment — only a staples multiple applied to a balance sheet at 4.5 times cash profit, with $4.5 billion of perpetual preferred and $3.9 billion of pod joint-venture minority interest standing ahead of the common. Deduct those properly and the defensible floor is about $26, corroborated by the $24.88 52-week low, by 10.3 times 2027 consensus earnings, and by a 3.5% dividend yield. Against a $36 base case that is roughly 1.3 to 1 from $31.12 — respectable, not asymmetric, and well short of the 2.8 to 1 the file carried.

Third, we would be joining a crowd. Consensus is $34.40 average and $37 median; JPMorgan went to $38 on 23 July and Bank of America put the name on its high-conviction list on 21 July. Our $36 sits inside the published range. A special-situation position pays for seeing what the market has not; here the market sees the parts perfectly well and is discounting the process — the leverage, the timing and the missing chief executive — which is precisely what we also cannot resolve.

Finally, the index-flow premise in the original file points the wrong way. Forced index selling hits the distributed company after the split, creating a discount in the coffee spin-off. It is not a tailwind for the parent beforehand. The real forced-seller trade in this situation is a future trade in the spin-off, and it is at least two or three quarters away.

So: wait for the wash-out, and be specific about it. Two developments convert this into an entry at any price: a named chief executive for the coffee company, or the registration statement filing that sets a record date. Either one turns an undated goal into a scheduled event and re-rates the reward-to-risk immediately. Absent those, one price does the same job — $28 or below, which is roughly 11 times 2027 earnings and puts the honest floor within about 8%, restoring genuine asymmetry. The 6 August 2026 second-quarter report, three days out, is the nearest thing to a trigger in either direction: a coffee-cost guidance cut could deliver that price, and a separation-timetable update could deliver the date. Watch it; do not front-run it.
interrogator_dossier:
# Keurig Dr Pepper (KDP) — Event Dossier

**Date of review:** 3 August 2026 · **Live price:** $31.12 (Nasdaq close, 31 July 2026 tape; market cap ~$42.3B)
**The event under examination:** a tax-free spin-off of the coffee business ("Global Coffee Co.") out of Keurig Dr Pepper, leaving a North American refreshment-beverage company ("Beverage Co.") behind.

This is not a judgement on whether Dr Pepper is a good business. It is a judgement on one question: is there a real, dated, binding corporate event that forces the market to re-price this company, and if the event does not arrive, what actually stops the stock from falling?

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC — how the story has evolved

The story began in August 2025, when Keurig Dr Pepper announced two things at once: it would buy JDE Peet's, the Dutch-listed global coffee group behind Jacobs, Douwe Egberts and Peet's, for roughly $18 billion in cash; and it would then split itself into two separately listed companies. Management's argument was that the combined company had become two businesses with almost nothing in common — a fast-growing North American drinks business (Dr Pepper, Canada Dry, Snapple, plus newer energy brands) bolted onto a slow-growing, commodity-exposed global coffee business — and that separating them would let each be valued on its own merits.

The buy side of that plan has been executed, and executed well. The tender offer for JDE Peet's was declared unconditional with 96.22% of shares tendered, settled on 1 April 2026, and rose to 97.75% after the post-closing acceptance window. Crossing 95% let the company start statutory buy-out proceedings under Dutch law, terminate the Euronext Amsterdam listing (last trading day 29 April 2026, delisted 30 April 2026), and implement a post-closing demerger — a restructuring step whose explicit purpose is to make the later separation possible. That is real, verifiable, completed corporate machinery, not a press release.

The sell side — the actual spin — has drifted. In late October 2025 management said the company would be "operationally ready to separate by end of 2026." Coverage of the February 2026 financing update still carried a year-end-2026 target, hedged by the phrase that timing depends on "achievement of key milestones, including appropriate leverage levels at each company, and supportive market conditions." By the 23 June 2026 announcement, the target had become "early 2027." That is one slip of roughly one to two quarters, and the language has moved from a date to a condition.

The second drift is in leadership, and it matters more than the calendar. The coffee chief executive seat has now emptied twice. Sudhanshu Priyadarshi, originally slated to run the coffee company, was replaced as chief financial officer in November 2025 and removed from that plan. Rafael Oliveira was named chief executive of the future Global Coffee Co. on the day the JDE Peet's deal closed in April 2026 — and told the company in June 2026 that he was leaving at the end of July for an outside chief executive role. The board has reopened the search, led by chairman Pamela Patsley, who will chair the coffee company's board after separation. Bank of America called the departure a setback specifically because the search has to restart ahead of a targeted 2027 spin.

**Read-through:** the acquisition is finished; the separation is not scheduled. A company cannot file a registration statement, run a roadshow, and set a distribution date for a business that has no chief executive.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS — testing the event, not the franchise

| Management claim | Verified evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| The JDE Peet's acquisition will close in the first half of 2026 | Settled 1 April 2026; 97.75% tendered; Amsterdam delisting 30 April 2026 | Delivered, on time |
| The company will separate into two listed companies | Board-approved; post-closing demerger implemented as the enabling step | Structurally in motion |
| Separation "by end of 2026" (Oct 2025 / Feb 2026) | Restated as "early 2027" on 23 June 2026 | Slipped |
| 2026 net sales of $25.9–$26.4 billion and constant-currency adjusted earnings-per-share growth in a low-double-digit range | Reaffirmed at first-quarter results on 23 April 2026 and again on 23 June 2026 | Holding, so far |
| First-quarter 2026 momentum | Net sales $3.98 billion, up 9.4% reported and 8.1% in constant currency; adjusted diluted earnings per share $0.39 | Delivered |
| Combined leverage of about 4.5 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation | Balance sheet at 31 March 2026 already shows $25.7 billion of total debt against $0.9 billion of cash, with roughly $18.0 billion of acquisition funding parked in current assets awaiting the April close | Consistent, and heavy |

The financial trajectory is respectable but the balance sheet has been transformed. Full-year 2025 revenue was $16.60 billion with reported earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of $4.19 billion. Consensus for 2027 — the first clean full year with coffee included — is roughly $29.9 billion of revenue, $7.64 billion of that same earnings measure, and $2.53 of earnings per share. At $31.12 the stock trades on about 12.3 times that 2027 figure, against large-cap packaged-food and drinks peers at roughly 17 to 20 times. So the optical discount is real.

**The forensic catch that a naive parts-valuation will miss.** The $18 billion was not funded with debt and common equity alone. Three separate claims now sit ahead of, or alongside, the ordinary shareholder:

1. **$4.5 billion of Series A convertible perpetual preferred stock**, co-led by Apollo and KKR with an anchor commitment from accounts advised by T. Rowe Price, upsized from $3 billion on 23 February 2026. It pays 4.75% a year, ranks senior to common stock for dividends and on liquidation with a $1,000-per-share liquidation preference, participates in common dividends on an as-converted basis, and is perpetual — it never matures. The investors have registration rights, meaning a defined path to sell into the market.
2. **A pod-manufacturing joint venture** into which an investor partnership backed by Apollo, KKR and Goldman Sachs Asset Management put roughly $4 billion for a 49% stake. This shows up as $3.9 billion of minority interest on the 31 March 2026 balance sheet. Note what was sold: 49% of the economics of K-Cup pod manufacturing — the single highest-margin node in the coffee business, the "blade" in the razor-and-blade model.
3. **Roughly $9 billion of new long-term debt plus about $5 billion of assumed JDE Peet's bonds.**

Add it up and something close to $36 billion of debt, preferred and minority claims sits between enterprise value and the common share. Any sum-of-the-parts that values the whole coffee business and subtracts only bond debt overstates per-share value by roughly $8.4 billion, or about $6 per share. This is the most important single number in the file.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Stable on operations, softening on the separation. Management has reaffirmed the 2026 outlook twice in three months, including on the same day it disclosed the loss of the coffee chief executive — a deliberate choice to separate operational confidence from separation confidence. The wording on the split has moved in one direction only: from "operationally ready by end of 2026," to a conditional year-end-2026 target, to "targeted for early 2027." Nobody has said the split is at risk; nobody has committed to a date either.

Tim Cofer, the chief executive, has said he will run the coffee business himself in the interim and become chief executive of Beverage Co. after the split. That is a candid admission that the coffee company is currently being run by someone whose future is at the other company.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY — high on operations, medium on timing

On the numbers, credibility is good. The company has met or exceeded consensus earnings estimates in each of the past four quarters, and the first quarter of 2026 came in ahead. On the transaction, credibility is excellent: an $18 billion cross-border tender that clears 96% and delists on schedule is hard, and they did it.

On separation timing, credibility is medium at best. One slip has already happened, the target is explicitly conditioned on leverage levels and market conditions the company does not control, and the leadership prerequisite has just been vacated for the second time. Reliability score on the event date: **Medium**.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three questions recur and none has a public answer:

- **How is the debt split?** Which company carries how much of the roughly $28 billion of net debt is the single largest determinant of what each share is worth, and it has not been disclosed. A coffee company loaded with the leverage is a very different security from a beverage company loaded with it.
- **What happens to the dividend?** The current $0.23 quarterly payout, $0.92 a year, yields about 3.0%. After the split it must be divided between two companies, and neither policy has been stated.
- **Where does the preferred and the pod joint venture land?** The convertible preferred was issued at the level intended to become Beverage Co.; the 49% pod-manufacturing stake is coffee-side economics. How these are allocated determines the real per-share value on both sides.

The pressure point management is not addressing is green-coffee cost. Elevated arabica prices have been compressing US coffee results all year, and the company now has vastly more coffee exposure than it did twelve months ago — at exactly the moment it wants to sell that business to the public market on a clean multiple.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**Red flags**

- The separation is undated. "Targeted for early 2027," conditioned on leverage and market conditions, is a goal, not a commitment (23 June 2026).
- The coffee chief executive seat is empty for the second time in nine months; the search restarted in June 2026. No registration statement for the coffee company has been filed.
- About $8.5 billion of non-common capital — $4.5 billion of perpetual preferred at 4.75% and $3.9 billion of pod-joint-venture minority interest — permanently reduces what the common shareholder owns. Selling 49% of pod manufacturing is selling the best margin pool in the coffee business.
- Leverage of roughly 4.5 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation makes the equity a levered call option: a 10% shortfall in profit combined with a one-turn multiple de-rating removes roughly a third of the share price.
- The dividend is a candidate for a reset at separation, and a 3%-yield shareholder base is not the natural owner of a levered, mid-split company.
- The index-flow leg of the thesis points the wrong way. When a spin happens, index funds that track the parent must mechanically sell the new company. That creates a discount in the coffee spin-off, not a gain in the shares you hold beforehand.

**Green flags**

- The hard part is done. The tender cleared 96.22%, settled 1 April 2026, reached 97.75%, delisted 30 April 2026, and the post-closing demerger — the legal step that makes the separation possible — has been implemented.
- The bridge loan was repaid early on 30 March 2026 out of preferred and joint-venture proceeds, removing short-term refinancing risk.
- Operating results are holding: first-quarter 2026 net sales up 9.4%, guidance reaffirmed twice, four consecutive quarters at or above consensus.
- Board-level commitment is visible in governance, not just words: a chairman designated for the coffee company's board, independent boards planned for both.
- The street has warmed rather than cooled — JPMorgan raised its target to $38 on 23 July 2026, Bank of America added the stock to its high-conviction list on 21 July 2026, and Barclays' own parts analysis points above the current price.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The financing tells you what management was worried about. Upsizing the preferred from $3 billion to $4.5 billion and selling half the pod business to private-credit sponsors, rather than issuing common stock, says the board judged the share price too low to sell — a bullish signal about their view of value, and a bearish one about the cost, because perpetual 4.75% preferred with registration rights and a liquidation preference is expensive, permanent capital.

The second signal is the phrase "appropriate leverage levels at each company." Read plainly, that is the company telling you the spin will not happen until each side can stand on its own balance sheet. With combined leverage near 4.5 times and free cash flow yield at roughly 3.7%, deleveraging to a level where two investment-grade companies can be carved out takes time. The date is a function of the balance sheet, and the balance sheet says "not soon."

The third signal is that the last three price-target raises came *after* the coffee chief executive resigned. The market is pricing the parts, not the process. That means the parts story is already consensus.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Trajectory: turning.** This is a company deliberately reconstructing itself into two different companies, and it is roughly halfway through.

**What the director must weigh before sizing:** the event is real but it is not scheduled, and the downside is not backstopped by anything hard. There is no deal-break price, no cash floor, no contractual payout — if the spin slips to late 2027 or is shelved, nothing catches the stock except a staples multiple on a levered balance sheet. The board file carried a floor of $28.50; that number is the 200-day moving average ($28.62), a chart level rather than a value backstop. The defensible floor, built from an adverse parts valuation with the preferred and minority claims properly deducted, is closer to $26 — near the 52-week low of $24.88, about 10.3 times 2027 consensus earnings, and a 3.5% dividend yield. Using the honest floor, the reward-to-risk from $31.12 is roughly 1.3 to 1, not the 2.8 to 1 the board file carried.

**Moat.** Narrow but genuine on the beverage side: Dr Pepper is the number-two carbonated soft drink brand in the United States and gaining share, supported by a direct-store-delivery distribution network that is expensive to replicate — an intangible-brand and scale-distribution moat. On the coffee side it is eroding: the Keurig razor-and-blade model faces unlicensed pod competition and declining single-serve volumes, and the acquired JDE Peet's business earns structurally lower margins than legacy Keurig, so the blended returns profile of the combined coffee company is below what Keurig alone once earned. Selling 49% of pod manufacturing narrows it further.

**Secular threat.** Manageable. Coffee and carbonated drinks are not being structurally displaced; the pressure is commodity cost and channel mix, which are cyclical and negotiable, not terminal. The cheapness here is a leverage-and-complexity discount, not a melting-ice-cube discount.
